Deck Nine had an impossible task in Before the Storm: Not just to create a prequel to a story-driven game with a cult fandom, but to do it with:

- A different game engine
- Different writers
- Different voice actors
- Different music
- No rewind mechanic

(Is now a good time to mention that Deck Nine's previous work includes "Neopets: The Darkest Faerie," some remastered Playstation ports, and a forgettable snowboarding franchise?)

In light of that, my expectations coming in were pretty low ... and they've been absolutely blown away. Episode 1 of Before the Storm isn't just true to the original game — as a one-to-one comparison, it's better than Episode 1 of the original Life is Strange. I feel exactly like I felt playing the first game, and I haven't felt that way since the first game ended more than 2 years ago. 

10/10 I'm not sure how this is even possible; go play it.
There are a few cringe moments, but I guess that comes with playing a teenage girl as a man. Nevertheless, if you enjoyed the original, the first episode is pretty solid.

Let's be real, if you played Life is Strange you're probably starved for any way to revisit our favorite heroines and would buy this game even if it were rated "Overwhelmingly Negative". The good news is that you don't really have to worry about that. This is a good game, though it lacks the ambitious exposition of the original. While Life is Strange violently plunged you into a world of secrets and conflict armed with a rewind button, Before the Storm focuses on smaller, and maybe more mundane happenings of Aradia Bay like teen angst, familial strife, betrayal, and the fast formed bond between two very different girls. Without the superpowers of her best friend Max, Chloe's tale in Before the Storm shapes up to be a much more intimate, personal, and human tale than the original.

After being so attached to the main game, I did not know what to expect when I heard the announcement of this one, frankly, I was not expecting much.
Especially after finding out the original voice actor for Chloe Price will not reprise her role.
But as soon as I clicked play, as soon as Episode 1's main track starts playing, I was completely immersed into the Life is Strange universe all over again.

It's like falling in love with your significant other all over again....except with a different voice.

Before the Storm, yet a Storm in and of itself.

Life is Strange blew me away back in March, to the point where I can't imagine a time where I didn't know the events of the game or how it shaped me as a person. Since the second Spanish Sahara left my headset, I couldn't pick up another game properly because I knew it wouldn't move me anywhere near how Life is Strange moved me... so I waited to play Before the Storm.

That was my first mistake.

Before the Storm is one of the most worthy prequels I've ever seen. It takes the qualities of the characters that I knew and loved from LiS and expanded on them in ways I couldn't fathom. It takes aspects of the story I thought I knew and turned it to be... new, fresh, and yet so familiar. It was like talking to an old friend, you know them and how they are, but there's something new from them that captures you.

Before I played, I expected Chloe to be moody and sullen with not much more character than she previously had, to the point where being in a school play seemed ridiculous, outlandish... impossible. Furthermore, I expected the characters that you are supposed to hate in the original game to be more of the same too, in particular regards to David, whom I expected to be a complete dick through and through. Yet he always seemed to have Chloe's best interested at heart, and given what I already knew, I took it far easier on him in BtS than I did in LiS. Finally, I also expected to hate the character of Rachel Amber. In Life is Strange, [spoiler]as she dies before the game even starts [/spoiler] you experience her character aspects through the eyes of Max, and realistically, she seems like an impossible person with very few flaws. I thought it'd be more of the same in Before the Storm, I thought she would be Little Miss Perfect, an 'Angel' as she's called by Chloe.

That was my second mistake.

This game has a story that's smaller than the events that transpire in the original game, obviously with there being only 3 episodes, there's less content. However, I made the huge mistake of thinking that because the story is smaller in scope,  [spoiler]as in, not threatening to wipe out an entire town,[/spoiler] the events that do happen have less of a lasting impact. This foolish mistake was brushed aside by the end of episode one when the fire starts. That scene will stick with me for many years to come. It will also teach me that just because events aren't displayed on a grand scale, doesn't mean that they are any lessoned in the terms of the overall narrative as I initially thought going into Before the Storm.

That was my third mistake. 

My final mistake, and arguably biggest mistake came in the expectations I had when it came to the music in this game. Having taken the gentler, more mellow sounds away from the original, I was worried that the punk-rock aspect of Chloe's character would through me off massively... yet it didn't. The difference in music only aided in the original and Before the Storm becoming two different entities for me that can easily stand by themselves. That being said... when the moment in the game became tense... or passionate, the music accommodating the scene is an understatement. For example, my overall favourite scene from this game, the one that'll stick with me permanently is the scene in episode 2, just after The Tempest play, where Rachel and Chloe are walking down the quite road over street lights. Taking You There by the Broods is pitch perfect for this moment. It utterly ruined me because of how happy both these characters were, [spoiler]especially considering what happens to them,[/spoiler] and how quickly it'd all change from that moment on. I suppose the issue I had going in was I expected more Spanish Sahara typed music.

That was my final mistake.

The overall theme of this review isn't persective as it was for my Life is Strange review... but the mistakes I made coming into it. On the topic of mistakes, I urge people to ask "is this game a worthy sequel?" rather than "is it better than Life is Strange?". I ask this because I can give you a real, down to Earth answer. You're God Damn right it is! 

TL;DR - Did a reverse Last of Us yet again... I couldn't lie to a character I care about as Joel does in TLoU. Characters made me feel like I was greeting an old friend, music made me tear up in some places (not quite Spanish Sahara style though), the choices I made felt impactful for Chloe and Rachel's relationship.

Life is Strange: Before the Storm is incredible and magical as it should be. It delivers on its promise of a captivating story that brings humanity to the idea of presumably senseless teen angst. It is a journey that explores the themes of loss, love, finding one's self, and whether the road to happiness ultimately lies in truth.

[b]Strange Beginnings[/b]

Announcing Before the Storm was definitely strange as the announcement for Life is Strange 2 had already been made. Moreover, while the original game was developed by Dontnod it was Deck Nine that made the announcement - a completely different studio (not France but US-based). I had my reservations especially as nothing suggested the game would include any sci-fi elements.

[b]Back To A Familiar Territory[/b]

Still, the game plays very similar to that of LiS. Instead of Max we play her best friend Chloe but this is before Max joining Blackwell. These are the very years Chloe was going through a lot while Max was away. It is nice to see a lot of new characters and many we met with Max now return. 

Gameplay-wise the approach is the same: we interact with objects and people and the more we do the closer we get to advancing to the next area or solving a puzzle. What amazes me how identical Before the Storm looks in terms of graphics, however, instead of Unreal it was the Unity engine utilised to bring the game to life. 

Decisions, again, matter and key events stop the gameplay asking you to make a choice. Chloe can regularly check her journal and see who texted her. Now, you do have to know that rewinding time is not an option in this game - this is as realistic as possible without any supernatural element. This may be a deterring factor for some.

[b]Tagging And Backtalking[/b]

Instead of taking photos Chloe uses a marker to do some graffiti. Finding the possible locations will be just as interesting as finding photo opportunities with Max and most of the achievements are related to this thing. Instead of time manipulation we now have backtalking - this is a solution offered to end (and thereby, win) an argument with someone. We have to listen carefully to what the "opponent" says and pick the closest sentence to that one when replying.

[b]Interpreting The Storm[/b]

This is Chloe's story with Rachel whose disappearance is key in LiS. The two become best friends and in case you wonder the things they go through involves a lot of drama, teenage angst. Since LiS set the bar already quite high I believe BtS cannot leave up to it, however, it's still a great story until we can get our hands on the sequel. Just don't have high expectations: this is Chloe not Max who was the embodiment of a cute and very positive protagonist. The anger in Chloe is sometimes a bit too much, still, this is a worthwhile journey till September.

This is probably the most thorough review I'll ever write on Steam, so I want to say some things before I start:

I'm only reviewing the first episode in its release state. I don't know yet if I'm going to update.
I'm going to refer to the original game as LiS, to this one as BfS.
LiS was a great game. People are hyped and give BfS 10/10 ratings, disregarding its obvious flaws. I would give it neither a thumb up nor a thumb down, but a "meh" rating.
BfS isn't developed by the same studio and you notice that extremely.
My review will get lots of thumbs down because the review system is broken. Giving a thumb down means telling that the review isn't helpful. People abuse the thumbs to vote down everything that doesn't agree with their opinion while voting up single sentence reviews that don't help anyone.

I'll try to keep spoilers out of my review as much as possible.


Let's take a look at some negative aspects, starting with technical stuff and proceeding into more "relevant" things:

- Graphics
While LiS was based on the Unreal Engine, BfS uses the Unity Engine. 
Believe it or not, but the simple graphics are a lot worse. I actually loved the art style of LiS, but in BfS I actually deleted every single screenshot I took (and I take a lot of screenshots) because they just weren't pleasant to look at. Textures often completely lack detail, anti-aliasing is non-existent (even on maxed out AA settings) which is actually a huge problem in this game, even though I usually don't care much about AA. All my screenshots were heavily
pixelated.

- Controls
Remember how you chose an action in LiS by holding the left mouse button and moving the mouse into the direction of the action? In BfS, you hold the left mouse button and use WASD to choose. In other words, in order to look at stuff or interact you need two hands now instead of only one. It's not a big deal, it just makes the game less comfortable at many scenes.

- Voices
You've probably heard already that Chloe has a new voice. You probably still have her accent from LiS inside your head. That's gone. Not a big deal, you could get used to that - the problem is that her new actress just isn't good. At  some points she sounds completely unmotivated and just talks her text down without any motivation at all. Near the end of the game you will also notice heavy breathing and hear clearly that she was standing to close at the microphone.
Chloe isn't the only character with a new voice, for example the famous angry David Madsen sounds really soft now.

- Animations
Lots of animations look really clunky and unnatural. I wanted to call an exorcist when Rachel was turning her head. In dialogues, characters often lack facial expressions. David gets angry and raises his voice, but his soft and calm expression stays. Until BfS I never noticed what a killer missing facial expressions can be.

- Paradoxes and other minor flaws
For example, there's a photo of pirate Chloe and pirate Max hanging in Chloe's living room. However, the Max with the eyepatch on the photo isn't the young Max we know from flashbacks, but the old Max you play as in LiS.
In Chloe's diary entry about a schoolmate she writes something such as "He's exactly like my class schedule. We have history, but no chemistry." You can read this while following the task "Go to your chemistry class."
The game is full of those details.

- Chloe's character
Alright, Chloe's a rebel. But sometimes it's just too much. In the beginning of the game you can look at a knife stuck inside a wooden wall and Chloe says something like "This looks exactly like the knife my mom didn't want to buy me for my birthday." She also likes tossing items just to the ground after using them, even if she borrowed them from a friend few seconds ago. I mean, come on...

- Dialogues
Some dialogues actually make me cringe. I won't go into details here due to possible spoilers. There's a new feature which enables you to argue with people. Everytime you have to persuade someone, just look out for the "arguing" sign and you know that's the way to go. It triggers a minigame like in Monkey Island, where your enemy delivers a statement and you have to counter with a fitting insult. Despite the fact that everyone beyond twelve years of age knows that you basically lose an argument as soon as you just start insulting your opponent, the arguing dialogues are just the worst in the game. They are just completely incoherent. You answer to a statement and suddenly your opponent starts about a completely different matter. After winning the minigame, it always seems to me like people stop arguing because they are annoyed by Chloes inability to argue, not because she "won". But of course Chloe had to be as rebel as possible and so it works in the game's context.
Furthermore, the reactions and answers of characters sometimes don't seem logical at all.

- Other characters
Except for Chloe and Rachel, the characters in this game mostly completely lack depth. You meet them, they start talking about a topic, you choose one or two answers, you go on with the game. I don't even remember what we talked about.
I didn't like Rachel at all until the ending of the episode, but that's just my personal opinion.

- Exploration
Remember how you strolled around in LiS, trying to find out everything about the world and its inhabitants? Trying to find motives for a good photo? It's almost non-existent in BfS. Chloe's a rebel and there's a stage play coming up at school. Everything you'll find are some posters about drug abuse and the upcoming stage play, without giving you any more information. Instead of taking photos, you can draw graffitis at walls now. There's a graffiti in every scene, so you just walk along walls until you find the spot to get your achievement.


Now, some more positive aspects:

+ Clothes
After the intro you have to change clothes. You can choose the outfit you want to wear during the episode. There are two different T-shirts in the base game, you unlock three more outfits if you buy the deluxe edition and you can play as classic Chloe (without blue hair) if you preordered the game.
- I probably don't have to mention that this feature is just a huge cashgrab for Square Enix. It's a neat feature anyway.

+ Soundtrack
Just like LiS, BfS has a nice indie rock soundtrack which fits well into the game.
- Remember the scenes in LiS, where you just enjoyed the scenery and a nice song to it? They are in BfS too, but somehow they don't seem to fit into the game or they were just executed half-heartedly. They are nice to have anyway.

+ Gameplay
Well, the gameplay won't surprise you. If you liked the gameplay of LiS and can live without time travel puzzles, you'll be satisfied.

+ New ideas
After the cool intro and the unfortunately very tedious middle part, the developers suddenly had their own ideas in the end and this is where the game finally shine. This might be a little spoiler, but there's a difference between Max and Chloe. While Max was very calm, Chloe can become very angry. At some part in the game it suddenly gets emotional, and instead of only showing Chloe's emotions, you actually get to live out Chloe's emotions. And it feels great.
The arguing minigame is actually quite exciting, despite it's obvious lack of logic.
For each graffiti, you can choose between two different messages which will also show up in your graffiti diary. Neat little gimmick.

+ The ending
Just like every LiS episode, episode 1 of BfS has a great ending. It didn't only leave me sitting with my mouth open, it actually sent a chill down my spine.


Conclusion:

If it wasn't for the first 20 minutes and especially the last 20 minutes of the episode (3.5 hours in total), I would actually give the game a clear thumb down. I give it a "meh" rating. It has very obvious flaws, but it's quite enjoyable if you're a LiS fan.

[h1]There are very few things that touched me the way [b]Life is Strange: Before the Storm[/b] did.[/h1]

Here, in the prequel to the original Life is Strange, we follow the story of young Chloe Price, a teenage rebel, struggling to let go of the pain that the death of her father and her best friend's subsequent abandonment have caused her. I find it kind of funny that a teenage drama could be so good...

Made by a different studio (Deck Nine), casting a new voice actress for Chloe, and finally unveiling the mysterious Rachel Amber, this game was feared by many fans to become a huge dissappointment - [b]however, it didn't[/b]. Instead, Deck Nine almost perfectly inherited the style of the original LiS, created a cast of compelling characters, both new and old, and told a story more grounded, tighly fitting the prequel's niche, and by that simply excelling everyone expectations. The chemistry between Chloe and Rachel is [i]electric[/i]; Chloe, her character and her loss felt so real to me. Finally, visuals, music and sounds are spot on.

While the adventure might seem quite short, spanning only 3 episodes, these episodes are long enough to deliver the intended experience without rushing the flow too much - except, maybe, the last episode. The writing is simply great; your actions don't feel like they are forced for the sake of having variation - the story, the choices I tailored it with, they all felt natural. The outcome of your choices may come in effect much later, affect the dialogue in small or big ways, and even open whole new gameplay parts. Some of your actions will yield positive or negative results in the later episodes, making you feel good that you, thankfully, did that thing back then, and not the other [spoiler](don't spend your hard-earned money on drugs, kids)[/spoiler].

Now, I have forgotten many details from the original Life is Strange, and maybe it's Before the Storm that makes a really good job, but while playing this prequel I almost completely let go of what I knew will happen, someplace and sometime else. After all, [i]life is about the journey, not about reaching death[/i], isn't it?

As far as I recall, the original Life is Strange didn't appeal to me as much as this game did. I don't remember seeing and feeling there such an electrifying chemistry between its characters, such joy of having my mind merge with the mind of the protagonist. After completion, I felt emotionally devastated and so sad that I can't spend some more time with the cast, enjoying more of the story and character of Chloe Price and Rachel Amber.

Concerning the gameplay: Chloe doesn't have superpowers, and she doesn't really need them - it's just an inventive Chloe Price vs. the World, who finds, breaks and/or backtalks her way through. Outside of dialogue, the game introduces small hubs that you can explore by walking around, looking, speaking, opening, picking, etc. stuff and leaving optional marks - Chloe's "trademark" graffitis, behind.

As for the cons - body animations can sometimes seem like a mess (come on, people don't walk like that). Facial animations, however, are among the best ones I've seen (Chloe's facial expressions - [i]oh, so good[/i]). And nothing in terms of bugs.

[h1]TL;DR:[/h1] [b]Overall,[/b] it's a beautiful and heartfelt experience of loss and friendship, with good story, great soundtrack and visuals. Developer Deck Nine followed DONTNOD in all of the best ways and have made an [i]amazing[/i] prequel that doesn't make you feel bad at all after revealing the mysteries of the original. I've played my share of episodic story-oriented games, but few of them felt particularly good - [i]and none felt as good as [b]Life is Strange: Before the Storm[/b][/i].

[h1]A Storm That Leaves You Silent[/h1]
[b]Some games entertain you. Some challenge you. But Life is Strange: Before the Storm? It reaches into your chest, grabs your heart, and refuses to let go. I thought I was prepared after playing the original Life is Strange, I was wrong. This prequel doesn’t rely on time travel or supernatural powers. Instead, it uses something far stronger: raw human emotion.[/b]

[h1]Chloe & Rachel – A Bond That Feels Too Real[/h1]
[b]This game tells the story of Chloe Price before she became the blue-haired rebel we knew, and her bond with Rachel Amber, a character who was only a mystery in the original game. Watching their friendship (and something deeper) grow feels so genuine that at times I forgot I was even playing a game. It doesn’t feel scripted, it feels lived. You feel their joy, their chaos, their recklessness… and eventually, their pain.[/b]

[h1]Farewell – The Episode That Broke Me[/h1]
[b]If the main episodes hurt, then Farewell was the final blow, a quiet, emotional nuke. Seeing Max and Chloe together one last time, knowing everything that’s about to happen in their future… it’s like watching the sun set while knowing a storm is right behind it. I’m not ashamed to say I had to pause the game just to process my feelings. It was beautiful, heartbreaking, and somehow comforting all at once.[/b]
[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Deep, emotional storytelling that feels painfully real
[*]Amazing soundtrack that carries every scene like poetry
[*]Beautiful character development, Chloe has never felt more human
[*]Farewell episode is one of the most emotional endings in gaming
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]No time rewind ability (You’ll wish you had it just to undo your own emotional damage)
[*]Game ends… and you’re left sitting in silence questioning life
[/list]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[b]Life is Strange: Before the Storm isn’t just a prequel, it’s a love letter, a goodbye, and a warning all in one. It teaches you that sometimes, life doesn’t need magic to be powerful. Sometimes, memories are enough to haunt you.
To those who’ve played the original, this is essential.
To those who haven’t, play this first, and prepare your soul.
Farewell, Chloe. Farewell, Rachel. And thank you… for the storm.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game. It's clearly inferior to [i]Life is Strange[/i], but in my eyes, it's more than just extended lore for unsatiated fans. 

Yes, the ending feels rushed, some dialogues sound forced, and the new “back talk” mechanic is clunky and unrewarding. 

But I was drawn in by how the game explores intimacy. Everyone violates others' private spaces — bedrooms, personal files, or deep secrets. Chloe Price, our protagonist, is a prime victim. She is methodically stripped of every personal landmark. Yet as players, we do the same to other characters — whether to satisfy curiosity or progress the story. Exploration becomes intrusion; our actions, interference. 

Meanwhile, we constantly feel watched. Messages urge us to reveal our location and activities. We're threatened with exposure on social media. Everywhere, signals insist our presence is unwelcome. As a primitive reaction, we mark our presence with graffiti — not to show off, but to preserve a sense of self. 

In that light, the story unfolds as a quest for personal space and authenticity, where every other character seems to have already failed. Every other character except Rachel, our freshly met accomplice and, if you want to, lover. I found their relationship convincing, supported by strong voice acting. I liked how the game lets intimacy grow between them in impersonal spaces, charged with collective memory: a national park, a junkyard, or an improvised scene from Shakespeare's [i]The Tempest[/i]. The gentle pacing, graphics, and music are on par with [i]Life is Strange[/i] and truly shine here. 

If you've played the original story, you know these moments merely stall the impending tragedy. The game doesn't explain how Rachel disappears, but it does give insight into why. In her painful quest, Chloe comes to question her most personal space: her imagination, haunted by the idealized dead dad. As much as it hurts, it makes her stronger. Rachel, on the other hand, has been protected from intrusion for too long. She's easy prey for a voyeuristic maniac.

[h1][b]Overview[/b][/h1]
Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a narrative adventure game developed by Deck Nine Games and released for PC in 2017. It serves as a prequel to the original Life is Strange, focusing on the relationship between Chloe Price and Rachel Amber before the events of the first game.

The game combines exploration, dialogue choices, environmental interaction, and character-driven storytelling rather than traditional action gameplay. Its main appeal comes from its emotional focus, believable character conflicts, and the way player choices influence conversations and relationships. It is primarily aimed at players who enjoy story-focused adventures, coming-of-age dramas, and slower-paced experiences where character development is more important than mechanical complexity.

[h1][b]Gameplay[/b][/h1]
Before the Storm follows a familiar adventure game structure: players explore locations, interact with objects, investigate environments, and make dialogue decisions that affect later scenes. The core gameplay loop is built around discovering information, understanding characters, and choosing responses during important conversations.

Unlike the original game, Chloe does not have a supernatural ability to alter time. Instead, the main dialogue mechanic is the "Backtalk" system, where players attempt to win arguments through carefully selecting responses. This provides some variety, but it is limited and does not reach the same level of strategic depth as the first game's rewind mechanic.

Controls are straightforward and work well on PC, with simple movement and interaction systems. There is very little difficulty, as the game focuses on narrative progression rather than challenge. Exploration rewards attention, with optional conversations and collectible items adding more context to the world, though the environments are generally small and heavily guided.

The pacing is a mixed element. The slower moments allow characters to develop naturally, but some sections feel stretched due to limited gameplay variety. The lack of major mechanical evolution means the experience depends almost entirely on how invested the player becomes in the story.

[h1][b]Story & World[/b][/h1]
The strongest aspect of Before the Storm is its character-focused writing. The game explores Chloe before the events of the original title, presenting a more vulnerable and emotionally complicated version of the character. The relationship between Chloe and Rachel is the central focus, and the game succeeds when it portrays their personalities, conflicts, and motivations.

The dialogue is often effective at creating realistic teenage conversations, though some scenes occasionally feel overly dramatic or less natural than the strongest moments of the series. The smaller-scale story allows more focus on personal relationships, but it also means the broader mystery and world-building are less developed.

The emotional impact depends heavily on the player's connection with the characters. When the writing is successful, it creates memorable and meaningful moments, but some pacing issues prevent the story from maintaining the same level of impact throughout.

[h1][b]Visual Presentation[/b][/h1]
The game maintains the series' distinctive painted visual style, prioritizing atmosphere and artistic expression over realistic graphics. Environments have strong identity, with detailed locations that support the mood of each scene.

Character models are serviceable but show their age, particularly in facial animations and movement. Expressions can sometimes appear stiff, which reduces the effectiveness of emotional scenes. Lighting and color choices are generally well handled and contribute significantly to the game's atmosphere.

The user interface is simple and functional, keeping attention on the story rather than menus or unnecessary design elements.

[h1][b]Audio[/b][/h1]
Music is one of the game's strongest features. The soundtrack complements the emotional tone of each scene, using licensed songs and original compositions to reinforce important moments.

Ambient sounds and environmental effects help create believable locations, while voice acting is generally strong. The main cast delivers convincing performances, although occasional dialogue delivery issues highlight weaknesses in some writing rather than the acting itself.

[h1][b]Performance & Technical Quality[/b][/h1]
The PC version runs well on modern hardware and does not suffer from major technical problems. Performance is generally stable, with reasonable graphics options and acceptable loading times.

Minor issues can appear, including occasional animation inconsistencies and visual glitches, but they rarely interfere with progression. The game is technically solid overall, although it does not provide extensive customization compared to larger modern releases.

[h1][b]Content & Replayability[/b][/h1]
The main story takes around 8 to 10 hours to complete, depending on exploration and how much optional dialogue the player views. Additional content is limited, with no multiplayer, cooperative modes, or significant endgame activities.

Replay value comes mainly from experiencing different dialogue choices and unlocking achievements. Players who enjoy comparing alternate outcomes may find reasons to return, but the game does not offer a large amount of content after the first playthrough.

[h1][b]Value for Money[/b][/h1]
The original release was sold as a complete episodic adventure with a relatively modest amount of content compared to full-priced games. Its value depends on how much a player values narrative experiences. For fans of story-driven adventures, the emotional focus and production quality justify the price, but players looking for extensive gameplay systems or long-term replayability may find it limited.

There are no microtransactions, and the additional episode content provides a complete experience rather than a fragmented one.

[h1][b]Pros[/b][/h1]
• Strong character development and emotional storytelling.
• Excellent soundtrack that enhances the atmosphere.
• Well-designed environments with a distinct artistic identity.
• Convincing voice performances from the main cast.
• Meaningful dialogue choices that encourage replaying scenes.

[h1][b]Cons[/b][/h1]
• Limited gameplay variety compared to other adventure games.
• Some dialogue and dramatic moments feel inconsistent.
• Facial animations and character models show technical limitations.
• Slow pacing can make certain sections feel unnecessarily long.
• Replay value is limited after completing the story.

[h1][b]Final Verdict[/b][/h1]
Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a carefully crafted character drama that succeeds because of its emotional writing, atmosphere, and strong performances. Its lack of mechanical depth and occasional pacing problems prevent it from reaching the highest level of narrative adventures, but it remains a worthwhile experience for players who appreciate thoughtful storytelling and character-focused games. It is best viewed as an intimate prequel that expands the world of Life is Strange rather than a major evolution of the genre.

[b]Final Score: 78/100[/b]

Despite being produced by a different developer, on its surface Before the Storm can be heralded as a true Life is Strange title, sharing many thematic elements with its predecessor. From the beginning of this prequel’s episodic trilogy, I was greeted with idyllic set pieces and familiar characters. The game’s expressive soundtrack sounded and swelled in the right moments, and though Ashly Burch did not reprise her role as Chloe Price, the voice acting from the entire cast was notably immersive. And yet, something was different during this second jaunt through Arcadia Bay. Some of its magic which had once left me transfixed, had faded, and at the end of this journey I felt more disillusioned than wishing to return.

Before the Storm’s most glaring weakness is the absence of the Rewind mechanic which had been central to the gameplay of Life is Strange. At their heart, the promise of both games revolves around the player’s ability to make meaningful decisions, or at the very least, the illusion of doing so. In the original title the reversal of time served as a tool to reinforce this illusion; players were encouraged to explore the immediate and diverse consequences of their actions, often in the form of dialogue options or interacting with objects. Rewind enabled players to methodically investigate the depth of a character’s range of reactions before making a final choice and moving the plot forward. Ultimately, Life is Strange saved its greatest rewards for players willing to understand the world and its characters thoroughly enough to deliberate the long-term ripples their decisions might create. Because of this, the denizens of Arcadia Bay felt increasingly fleshed-out and alive; and the freedom provided to the player, to take a handful of steps down each possible path, was enough to demonstrate the relevance of their agency. It was insignificant that most of the paths crossed and merged just as they curved out of sight. Like all magic, what mattered was the illusion and that we as spectators were enticed enough to accept it. While Before the Storm introduces the enjoyable new dialogue mechanic, Backtalk, it presents no substitute for the utility of the Rewind mechanic in maintaining the illusion of meaningful choice. It is perhaps for this reason that so many decisions in this sequel felt pointless, linear, like being dragged along on a string. Without a means for the player to prove otherwise, it was often as if every dialogue option were essentially the same, as if player input were irrelevant, unwanted, and the story was content enough to continue moving on its own. 

Compounding the issue is the setting of Before the Storm as a prequel to the original game. Interactions with nearly every returning character felt partially futile and fabricated. Despite the radical changes or growth a character may undergo in Before the Storm, he or she will inevitably become the same flawed person Max interacts with three years later in Life is Strange. This certitude caused many well-known characters to appear either static or ingenuine and, though I thoroughly explored every side-arc of the original title, while playing Before the Storm I found myself avoiding interactions with the main cast altogether. Likewise, because the protagonist of this game, Chloe Price, is herself a nuanced character in Life is Strange, even many of Before the Storm’s most climactic decision points feel disappointingly ineffectual. What is perhaps the game’s strongest narrative moment takes place in the closing scene of the game, after the player has made their final decision. It is a true shame that in a game built around choices, many of the most well-defined and memorable aspects of the story unfold while the player is deprived of control.

From a narrative standpoint, Before the Storm struggles occasionally with pacing and cloying plot clichés; it boasts a story and visual style which manage to capture the style of Life is Strange, but not its spirit. The journey through the episodic story is dishearteningly mediocre, marred by contrivances and poor characterization, and irksomely weak in terms of player agency. As someone who was enraptured by the contemplative melancholy of the original game, I was left largely disappointed and would have preferred to experience the contents of this prequel in the pages of a novella or in a similar medium better suited for its linearity and narrative constraints. If developer Deck Nine opts to prolong our venture in Arcadia Bay with a future title, let us hope they are more careful to revitalize the depth, wonder, and soul Dontnod had originally breathed into their world.

Life is Strange: Before the Storm (BTS) is an interactive story-focused game developed by Deck Nine and published by Square Enix. It was initially released on 1 September 2017. Before the Storm is a prequel to Life is Strange, in which the story focused on the relationship between Max Caulfield and Chloe Price. Meanwhile, BTS focuses on Chloe Price and her newfound friendship with Rachel Amber following Max's departure from Arcadia Bay. This review will focus on the BTS story, before comparing and reviewing the connection from BTS to the original Life is Strange. Finally, this review will discuss the standard and deluxe editions.

[h1] [b] Story [/b] [/h1]

The story in BTS was an absolute roller coaster. I completed all episodes, minus ''Farewell'', the bonus episode in 12 hours. I took my time as well as admiring the environment, listening to the soundtrack, and interacting with all characters.

The story was expertly structured to commence with a situation (i.e. Chloe's tenure at Blackwell Academy), her newfound friendship in Rachel and how their friendship spiralled into chaos and excitement. Each episode ends with a ''big bang'' where you are left questioning your actions and decisions and the consequences of those actions. For example, all episodes utilise the deer in its spirit animal form to symbolise a connection between BTS and the original game, where we question, ''is the spirit animal Rachel in some form?''. I find these subtle elements to be a key figure in presenting the story.

BTS connects really well to Life is Strange. Throughout the story, there are many references that you encountered in the original game. For example, the original game briefly discussed Chloe, Joyce, and the accident with Chloe's father. In BTS, the story drives you to understand what happened on a day-by-day level rather than flashbacks. These connections, among others, really made this game an excellent piece because of the call-backs to the original game. A second example, the original game discussed Rachel Amber has a post story with missing posters, BTS drives that story. In other words, it definitely is a prequel and both stories make sense.

Regarding voice acting for Rachel, I note that Deck Nine hired a different actor to portray Chloe. While the new actor (rather than the original from the original game) had a softer voice, Chloe is notably younger in this game and I think it worked very well. The actor did really well in terms of expressing emotion and showcasing the different voice tones to the different aspects within the game.

[h1] [b] Deluxe Edition DLC [/b] [/h1]
I do not recommend purchasing the deluxe edition. The edition contains "Farewell", the bonus episode that follows BTS. I was extremely interested in completing the episode, however the game crashed three minutes into the episode. This crash issue appears to be an issue for many other players who reported the crash. Unfortunately, it hasn't been fixed by Deck Nine. I instead, watched the DLC on YouTube and I absolutely recommend watching it on Youtube. It is both an emotional and excellent finale to the Chloe and Max story. I watched the episode in about 90 minutes.

[h1] [b] Conclusion [/b] [/h1]
I had an absolute blast playing BTS. It continued and connected a beautiful storyline in Life is Strange and expanded on the story to provide an understanding to the user on the situation of Rachel Amber. The sound and dialogue, coupled with the choices that dictate how the story progresses, makes this prequel an absolute must-buy. For AUD$22.49, I recommend this game at full price.

[h1] [b] Pros [/b] [/h1]
	· Diverse range of characters with disparate and familiar personalities
	· Interactive elements that enable your choices to dictate the story
	· Soundtrack, which is both excellent, relaxing, and emotional to listen in the game
	· Emotional connection, this game really does allow you to relate to the characters and experience an emotional connection with the characters
	· Storyline call-backs to the original Life is Strange.

[h1] [b] Cons [/b] [/h1]
	· Disappointing crash in ''Farewell'' that didn't allow me to play the final episode.

For a game I waited years to play I couldn't be more disappointed with Life is Strange: Before the Storm. 

This story was marketed as being about Chloe's descent from a sweet carefree straight A student (except for a B in PE) to the bitter, abrasive, rebellious and emotionally damaged person we came to know in the original Life is Strange. However as it turns out that's basically who Chloe is at the start of Before the Storm. Therefore the story has no real character development.

What was sold to us as a character study turned out to be "Another Arcadia Bay Mystery!" only this time with bland characters, lazy twists and a plot riddled with holes.

(Spoilers ahead)

The story ultimately revolves around Rachel Amber with Chloe as little more than our window into her contrived and absurd world. 

In the first Life is Strange game Arcadia Bay has all but forgotten Rachel Amber with the exception of her best friend Chloe who is still desperately pasting missing person posters of her all over town. In Before the Storm we're told that Amber is in fact the DA's Daughter! So we're to believe the Ambers just gave up looking for her? Furthermore why would Nathan and Jefferson be so stupid as to target such a high profile individual. The only way this element of the story could possibly make sense is if after the events of Before the Storm Rachel's father was in jail, which actually would make a whole lot of sense (but isn't how things work out).

I really wasn't invested in the bizarre story of Rachel's junkie birth mom and it's ultimately pretty ridiculous when you get right down to it. Her dad ultimately hires Damon, a drug dealer to kidnap the woman and shoot her up with heroine just to prevent her from meeting her daughter. In order to bribe him into doing this he offers to destroy evidence from a crime Damon committed. Why would he go to such lengths, risking his career and freedom just to stop a simple meeting between Rachel and her biological mother?

Worse still the whole premise conflicts with the original Life is Strange. That story never intended to imply Chloe had been caught up in any sordid and intriguing conspiracies prior to meeting Max. Yes she was a punk, she hung out with drug dealers but if she'd gotten mixed up in a kidnapping and murder plot you'd think that's something she'd mention to Max as they find themselves in ANOTHER KIDNAPPING AND MURDER PLOT.

There are similar problems with the way Frank is woven into the story. It's to be expected that Frank would make an appearance in this game but his role in the story seemed unfitting for the character. In Life is Strange Frank is a shifty and violent drug dealer with a very well hidden soft side. In Before the Storm he's borderline heroic, constantly stepping in to save Chloe, including risking his life for her in the final confrontation with Damon (which also makes for an unsatisfying deus ex machina). It's even implied that Frank went so far as to kill his former boss to save Chloe. 

This makes the character and plot completely dissonant with Frank's arc in the original Life is Strange. If it had ever been imagined that he and Chloe had such a long and storied past the details really should have come up. Frank should have been pointing out the number of times he's saved Chloe's ass when demanding she pay him the money she owes. He shouldn't have just been pissed at her for stiffing him he should have felt downright betrayed.

Ironically the one area that would make sense to explore when it comes to Frank, his relationship with Rachel isn't so much as touched on. That they were actually lovers is a surprise to Chloe in Life is Strange but they could have at least had them meet, maybe sprinkled in some hints for dramatic irony. 

Before the storm also tries and spectacularly fails to capture the original game's theme of subverting your initial impression of different characters. Whereas the original game took the time to develop people like Frank, David, Nathan and Mark Jefferson and then revealed an entirely different and unexpected (but completely believable) side of them the prequel simply throws in cheap twists for poorly thought out characters. 

The most contrived of all is Eliot. Out of nowhere he reveals himself not to be a friend of Chloe with a rather obvious crush but in fact a controlling and violent stalker. The entire scene was completely pointless. They just threw it in in a feeble attempt to be shocking. It doesn't help that in this role Eliot is painfully reminiscent of Warren from the original game.

Even the scenes of Chloe hallucinating or imagining William were ultimately a waste. They were heartfelt, surreal and beautifully voice-acted, but they had no impact on plot or character. They’re just meant to tug at our heartstrings and nothing more.

Possibly the only satisfying part of the whole game was the "bonus episode" but that really should have been the opening. It's also problematic story-wise. The twist reveals that the whole chapter takes place in the time between when William left to pick up Joyce from the grocery story and when she returned to inform Chloe and Max that he'd died in a car accident. This seems more than a little implausible as the episode runs well over an hour and starts with Max and Chloe seemingly having been busy cleaning out her room for hours more.

At this point I'm not sure if the game was a wasted opportunity or just a bad idea from the start.

Life is Strange: Before the Storm serves as a prequel to the first Life is Strange game, focusing on Chloe Price's life before the events of Arcadia Bay. While the concept had potential particularly in exploring the much discussed relationship between Chloe and Rachel Ambe the execution is not really good.

One of the game's most questionable elements is its attempt to provide Chloe with a gameplay mechanic comparable to the supernatural abilities from the first game. In this case, it's a "backtalk" feature, where Chloe argues her way through conversations using sarcastic comebacks. Unfortunately, this mechanic feels forced and awkward. It seems to be there just for the sake of having something "special", but it lacks credibility. The idea that a teenager could argue her way past adults in serious situations borders on absurdity. Instead of strengthening her character, it often ends up making her feel like a caricature of rebellious teen.

That same tone carries over into other parts of the game. Collectibles take the form of graffiti, which are presumably intended to be edgy or humorous, but instead come off as cringeworthy and poorly thought out. Rather than deepening the player's connection with Chloe or the world, they seem to underline how one dimensional her character is portrayed here.

The central plot revolves around Chloe's evolving relationship with Rachel Amber something that was shrouded in mystery in the first game and had a lasting emotional impact. Unfortunately, Before the Storm doesn't manage to add much depth to this dynamic. Rachel is portrayed inconsistently, sometimes as magnetic and inspiring, other times as manipulative or downright cruel. The game briefly teases the possibility of supernatural elements connected to her character, hinting at something more significant, but it never follows through. This results in a buildup that leads nowhere, leaving confusion rather than intrigue.

It's worth noting that this prequel was developed by a different studio than the original. While it does a decent job staying close to the original's tone and lore, it ultimately feels like a story that didn't need to be told. Instead of offering new insights or emotional weight, the game often feels like a summary of Chloe's life rather than a fully realized narrative. At times, it seems like the writers were trying to hit a checklist of emotional beats without giving them the time or development they needed.

The game is split into just three episodes, which in itself isn't a problem, but it ends up cramming too much into too little time. As a result, many moments feel rushed, underdeveloped, or driven by convenient plot twists. The characters, aside from Chloe and Rachel, barely get enough screen time to leave an impression. Their actions often seem exaggerated or unrelatable, and it's hard to see them as believable people rather than narrative tools.

There are moments when the game quiets down and allows a more grounded portrayal of Chloe moments where it explores her grief, confusion, and vulnerability in ways that feel sincere. These glimpses are the best part of the game, to be honest, and offer a rare emotional connection. Sadly, they are short lived and quickly overshadowed by the game's louder, less convincing dramatics.

In the end, Life is Strange: Before the Storm feels like it misses the essence of what made the original impactful. It wants to expand on a beloved character and a meaningful relationship, but doesn't quite know how to do so without falling into clichés or sacrificing coherence. Fans of the first game may find some value in revisiting Chloe's world, but overall, this prequel doesn't do much to enrich the series as a whole.

A simple premise can be a difficult one. For Before the Storm, Deck Nine were tasked with simply explaining how Chloe Price had become so enamored with Rachel Amber before the events of the original Life is Strange.

Many were skeptical of this angle, since in the original Life is Strange, Rachel is little more than a plot device that allows Max and Chloe to rekindle their friendship. The entire point of her character in that game was that she wasn't actually a character. So Deck Nine had the unenviable task of proving a passionate fanbase wrong by delivering a character that lived up to her almost mythological status.

And boy, did they knock it out of the park.

After a brief prologue during which Chloe first runs into Rachel at a DIY rock show, we are immersed in Chloe's troubled existence. Before the Storm takes place several years before the events of the original game, and about 2 years after Chloe's father died in a car accident, shortly after which her best friend Max moved to a different state.

The initial hour of the game establishes Chloe's state of mind in this period of her life. From the unprocessed trauma of her father's death to her enduring frustrations about losing touch with Max, Chloe struggles to keep herself afloat in a world that has already moved on. The game is intentionally confrontational in its exposition; through the eyes of Chloe, you get into conflict with nearly every adult you encounter in these early stages of the game, and some of your schoolmates aren't any nicer. There's additional background information delivered through Chloe's journal and text messages, which makes it all the easier for the player to empathize with her.

Not only does this help us get on board with a character that was, in the first game, oft seen as petty and selfish; it also sets the stage for Rachel Amber to swoop in as a savior. The first scenes with Rachel are the opposite of most of Chloe's interactions up until that point: she's on your side, she's sympathetic to you, and she's interesting to talk to. In this first act, the writers make it so that Rachel not only overwhelms Chloe, but also the player.

Of course, Rachel and Chloe's relationship soon becomes more complex, not just because conflict makes for a better story, but also because this prequel is by its nature required to conclude in a way that corresponds with the not-so-rosy events of the main game. More on that in a bit.

Though the main story thread in Before the Storm is the friendship between Chloe and Rachel, there are more plotlines at play. These involve mature themes such as drug dealing, dark family secrets, stalking and PTSD, but these story elements are handled with much more subtlety than in Life is Strange. In that game, we got on-the-nose, at times charicatural depictions of bullying, suicide, euthanasia, murder, and a bunch of other unsavory topics. While it made for an exciting game, it was so over-the-top that it could fatigue the player.

In Before the Storm, there is much more focus on character development. Primarily between Chloe and Rachel, but also between Chloe and other people, like Joyce, David and even Frank. 

This is a double-edged sword, as the first 2 Episodes revolve so heavily around Chloe and Rachel that the other plot threads seem like red herrings, until they're suddenly not. 

Deck Nine fulfills its initial promise by the end of the second episode, when the relationship between Chloe and Rachel reaches its zenith during and shortly after a school play. The school play - an unconventional adaptation of Shakespeare's 'The Tempest' - features the absolute peak of Deck Nine's writing, and I would argue the best writing in the entire series. Shakespeare's play becomes a metaphorical commentary on the relationship between our main characters; a thought-provoking, multi-layered commentary that is by itself seldom seen in video games. This is elevated all the more by Deck Nine disarming the player right before the climatic scene by distracting them with 'gamey' gimmicks, allowing for maximum emotional impact. If you want a perfect example of ludonarration - using gameplay mechanics to enhance and enrich the story - then look no further.

Yet, therein also lies the issue with Before the Storm. After this highest of highs, the game still has one episode and a bit to go. At this point in the story, though, the initial 'thesis' has already been completed: we now understand why Chloe was so smitten with the enigmatic Rachel Amber. So, out of necessity, the story then shifts focus to a subplot concerning the Amber family history, which takes up most of the third episode. While there are plenty of touching, emotional moments and memorable scenes in this final act, it does feel like a downgrade from the initial premise of the game.

This shift in focus may in part be motivated by Before the Storm's secondary obligation: it needs to tie in to the main game, which, for all its focus on chaos theory, has a lot of events that are set in stone.

There are more consequences to said approach. Some of the character development feels out of tune with what we see in the original Life is Strange. This may sound like a complaint, but it is not that simple: in Life is Strange, many of the characters are, even by the admission of its creators, stereotypes, at least in the beginning of the story. Characters like David, Nathan and Victoria start out as one-dimensional, and only gradually develop some depth as the plot evolves. The success of the character development in that game is a different discussion.

What this means for Before the Storm is that, depending on your choices, the character development is at times too good to be connected to the original game. Stereotypes can still be found, but the initial character depth is already a league above what we saw in Life is Strange, let alone the development some of the characters go through across the three episodes. To name an example, the David we see at the beginning of Life is Strange is a downgrade from the David we (may) see at the end of Before the Storm, even though the latter game takes place years prior. It is, however, tough to call this an error in judgment when it is in many ways the result of Deck Nine frankly having a much better writing staff than Dontnod (a fact that becomes even more clear when you compare any dialogue between both games.)

The 'incompatibility' between both games even extends to a more meta level. Life is Strange taught us that minor changes in a timeline may have large, unforeseen consequences - the butterfly effect. And yet we are to believe that the choices we make in Before the Storm - some of which cause dramatic shifts in the psychology of certain characters and/or their relation to other characters - have absolutely no bearing on the events leading up to Life is Strange.

As you can see, Life is Strange: Before the Storm leaves a lot of room for contemplation, which is a testament to the depth of the story. I have little hesitation calling Before the Storm the best game in the series and one of the best stories told in gaming. It is not perfect, but it [i]is[/i] a fine example of how to properly use a video game as a mature storytelling medium without ending up as a laughable QTE circus like Heavy Rain.

The game's biggest weakness is that it is a prequel, and you might be better off forgetting about Life is Strange proper during your time playing. It will still leave you with plenty to ponder over as it is easy to relate certain parts of the story and characters to your own life, leading to a unique perspective that may even evolve over time as you gain more life experience. If you are receptive to this type of storytelling, Before the Storm will stay with you for years after the final credits roll.

I played this game years ago, and I just replayed it recently... and wow. That’s the only word that keeps echoing in my head. This game is beautifully written. It is such an emotionally rich experience that adds so much weight and depth to the original Life is Strange in ways I didn’t think were possible originally.

If you loved the original game, this one is essential. It brings new life to familiar faces and sheds light on characters you thought you already understood. Chloe Price becomes more than just the rebellious best friend because now you actually feel her pain, her longing, her confusion, and everything through her eyes. And Rachel Amber? She’s no longer just a name whispered through the halls of Blackwell. This game makes her real. Vivid, charismatic, broken, bright. You understand why people were drawn to her, why her absence mattered so much in the first game. She is not just a plot device anymore, she’s an actual person you grow to love. And Nathan... oh, Nathan. I won’t spoil a thing, but replaying this made me see everything in a different light. His portrayal here adds so much nuance to who he is and how he got there. It’s subtle, it’s heartbreaking, and it honestly made me feel things I didn’t expect.

Now, the writing is poetic without trying too hard, the soundtrack is perfect (as usual); raw, indie, moody, and unforgettable. And the visuals, while stylized, are deeply atmospheric. Every scene OOZES emotion. Every line of dialogue feels like it means something. This game hurts in all the right ways. And somehow, through all the chaos and aching emotion, there’s this quiet beauty that sticks with you long after the credits roll.

I can’t recommend this game enough. Whether you’re returning to Arcadia Bay or visiting it for the first time, this story WILL wrap around your heart and stay there for many, MANY years. Play it. You won’t regret it.
